This paper develops a continuous-time general equilibrium model where investors&apos; growth expectations are driven by associative memory retrieval. Because belief formation depends on the infinite-dimensional history of returns and volatility, the valuation equation yields a path-dependent partial differential equation. I solve this system using a causal LSTM-based Deep BSDE solver validated against an exact analytic benchmark to five decimal places. Empirically, I construct a strictly backward-looking Memory Resonance Index (MRI) that identifies crash anchors using only historical price paths. In China&apos;s retail-dominated CSI 300 index (2005--2025), a one-standard-deviation increase in daily MRI predicts a 0.21 percentage point decrease in next-day excess returns (t=-4.71). The effect survives flexible controls for nonlinear momentum and volatility, and a 500-draw random-anchor placebo test confirms that the crash-detection algorithm is essential (p<0.002). In the U.S. S&P 500, however, MRI has no incremental predictive power and is spanned by VIX and valuation ratios. The model rationalises this contrast: associative memory generates significant contemporaneous valuation discounts in price levels, while market frictions and limits to arbitrage dictate whether these cognitive distortions translate into predictable return dynamics.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7355192\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7331065\", \"title\": [\"Public Transit Path Choice Modeling with Behavior Driven Preference Learning: An Interpretable Framework\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Public transit path choice behavior modeling is fundamental to travel demand analysis and transit guidance strategies. The type of research is a quasi-experiment with a three treatment counterbalanced design research design. The instruments used: (1) students 'initial mathematical ability tests, (2) tests of students' mathematical problem-solving abilities with the Pythagorean Theorem material. Inferential data were performed using covariance analysis (ANACOVA). The samples of this study were 32 students each from three experimental classes selected by purposive sampling.
